prompt: A weekly load that feeds the leadership dashboard silently dropped one of its sources last Tuesday. You discover it on Friday afternoon and decide to raise it at Monday's standup instead. What breaks first over that weekend, and who pays for the delay?
criteria: Names a decision someone makes on the stale numbers before Monday
States that the cost of the slip grows with every day it is unreported
Identifies the risk that someone else finds it and reports it first
Says what could still be salvaged by speaking on the Friday

prompt: It is Wednesday afternoon and you have just worked out that a migration promised for the end of the month will land about two weeks late. Write the short message you send to the sponsor today.
criteria: Leads with the date moving rather than with the explanation
Gives a revised date, or a date by which a firm date will exist
Offers at least two options the sponsor can choose between
Stays under five sentences with no apology preamble

prompt: Put these steps in the order you would take them on the day you realise a committed deadline is going to be missed.
items: Send the agreed plan in writing to everyone downstream
Tell the owner the date has moved and walk them through the options
Notice the task is behind and confirm how many days are at stake
Draft two recovery options and price each one in scope and time

prompt: True or false: sitting on a known two-week slip until you have a confirmed recovery plan spares the stakeholder unnecessary noise. Say why.
criteria: Says the stakeholder loses days they could have spent re-planning
Names the trust cost when they hear about it from someone else
States that options can be offered before a plan is confirmed
Separates a rough date with a caveat from giving no signal at all

prompt: A product manager asks how much revenue a weekend checkout bug cost. You have order counts for the affected hours but no record of the sessions that failed. Give the answer you would say out loud, with the number and how sure you are of it.
criteria: Gives a low and a high figure rather than one number
Attaches a stated confidence or likelihood to that range
Names the single unknown that drives most of the spread
Says what would narrow the range and how long that would take

prompt: Someone is asked how many active users the product has and replies: "It depends what you mean by active, the event data has gaps in April, and the mobile SDK undercounts, so I'd rather not give a number until I've dug in." Critique that reply.
criteria: Points out that the reply contains no figure at all
Says caveats belong after a number, not in place of one
Rewrites it as a figure with a range and a stated definition
Keeps only the caveat that would change what the asker does

prompt: You are about 80 percent sure that a data-quality problem touches between 2 and 5 percent of rows, and a director asks you how big it is. Which reply gives them the most to act on?
options: Somewhere between 2 and 5 percent of rows, and I'd be surprised if it fell outside that
Roughly 3.4 percent of rows
I can't say anything until the audit finishes next week
Hard to know — there are several known issues with that data

prompt: Which of these turn a rough estimate into something a decision-maker can actually use? Select all that apply.
options: Stating an explicit low and high figure
Saying how confident you are that the truth sits in that range
Listing every assumption you made before you state the number
Naming the one input that would move the number most
Rounding to a precision that matches what you actually know
Quoting the figure to two decimal places to show the work was careful

prompt: Your lead says: "Keep all six dashboards in the first release — we can't drop any of them." Two of the six depend on a data source that will not exist for another month. Write your reply.
criteria: Names which specific items you would move out of the release
States what the lead gives up if those items are cut
Prices the alternative — a later date, or more people on it
Ends by asking for a decision rather than registering a complaint

prompt: When is proposing a scope cut the wrong response to a schedule squeeze, and what do you put on the table instead?
criteria: Names a case where the item at risk is the point of the project
Says the tradeoff belongs to whoever owns the outcome, not to you
Gives an alternative such as re-sequencing or asking for help
States that a silent slip or a weekend push is still not the answer

prompt: Match each squeeze to the move that fits it.
left: The deadline is fixed by an outside commitment
The full list matters more than the launch date
One item waits on a source that arrives next month
Every item is required and the date cannot move
right: Hold the list and move the date
Split into two phases with that item in the second
Ask for another person, or knowingly drop a quality step
Cut the lowest-value items and say which ones went

prompt: Complete the sentence that turns a scope problem into someone else's decision rather than your private slip: "Here's what I'd ___, and here's what that ___ you."
Someone asks you for "a dashboard for churn". Explain what you would pin down before writing any code, and name the later argument each one heads off.
criteria: Names the artifact that will exist at the end in concrete terms
Names the one person who accepts it as finished
Names a condition that would make the output wrong
Ties at least one item to a revision cycle it prevents

prompt: A ticket carries this as its finish line: "Done when the numbers look right and the requester is happy with it." Pull that apart and give a version you would agree to.
criteria: Points out that looks right names no check against anything
States that satisfaction has no end point, so revisions never stop
Adds a figure or source the output must reconcile against
Names a single person who does the accepting

prompt: Which of these belong in a finish line agreed with the requester before any work starts? Select all that apply.
options: The exact artifact that will exist when the work stops
The named person who checks it and accepts it
A known figure the output has to reconcile against
The list of every function and query you plan to write
The condition under which the result would be wrong
The tool or language you intend to build it in

prompt: You have been handed a vague request. Order these four moves as you would make them in the kickoff conversation.
items: Restate the whole thing back and get a yes in writing
Name the single person who will accept the result
Ask what decision the output is going to feed
Agree the figure or check the output must match

prompt: An interviewer asks what you did on your last project, a pipeline rewrite. Give the answer in under ninety words: the situation, what you did, and what came of it.
criteria: Opens with the situation and what was wrong with it
States what you personally did, separate from what the team did
Closes on a result carrying a specific measured number
Claims no credit for the parts other people delivered

prompt: A manager drafting your review writes "cut report runtime by 90%". The real figure was 35 percent, and a colleague did the indexing that produced most of it. Write what you say to them.
criteria: Corrects the number to the one you can defend if challenged
Names the colleague's contribution rather than absorbing it
Keeps the part of the claim that is yours instead of waving it all off
Says why the accurate figure is still worth putting in the review

prompt: One line of this account of a past project undermines the rest of it. Which line, and why?
lines: Our weekly finance report took six hours and failed overnight most weeks.
I profiled the job and found one join scanning the full history every run.
I rewrote it to read only the partitions that had changed.
Single-handedly, I saved the company millions of dollars a year.
Runtime went from six hours to twenty minutes and it has not failed since.
why: It swaps a measurable result for an unverifiable claim and takes sole credit for it. The runtime figure on the next line is the part a listener can check, and the inflated line makes them doubt it.

prompt: A hiring manager who has heard a lot of overclaiming asks what your reliability work achieved. Which phrasing survives their scepticism?
options: I dramatically improved the reliability of our reporting
Failed runs went from about four a month to zero, and stayed there for a quarter
I owned the reporting reliability workstream
Reliability improved by more than 400 percent

prompt: Two documents propose the same architecture. One lists only the chosen approach; the other also lists the approaches that were rejected and why. Explain why the second is easier to review.
criteria: States that a reader cannot disagree without knowing the alternatives
Says the rejected options reveal which constraints were weighed
Names the cost of re-arguing the same option months later
Ties the choice to a consequence the reader can attack directly

prompt: You circulate a document that opens with the proposed table layout and never states what is wrong today. What breaks first once people start commenting?
criteria: Says reviewers argue over details instead of over the goal
Names the case where the wrong problem gets solved entirely
States that the choice cannot be judged without the problem
Says what the opening paragraph should have contained instead

prompt: Match each section of a design document to the question a reader opens it to answer.
right: Which one we picked, and on what grounds
What gets harder or more expensive once we do this
What is broken today, and for whom
What else we could have done, and why we did not

prompt: True or false: the downsides of the chosen approach are best left out of a design document, since naming them invites readers to reject the proposal. Say why.
criteria: States that reviewers find the unnamed downsides anyway
Says naming the consequences is what makes the document reviewable
Notes the credibility cost when a hidden cost surfaces after the fact
Separates stating a cost from arguing against the choice
